# Tail-root Jensen for arbitrary dominated submeasures

This extends `candidate 82d7337f4dd32126`. It does not
assume that a selected submeasure is uniform, convexly supported, or constant
on a fiber. It supplies a precise three-fiber peeling criterion, not a proof
that this criterion always holds.

## 1. The dominated-submeasure theorem

Let C subset R^n x R^d be a convex body, d>=1, and let mu be its unnormalized
mixed d-volume, with positive fiber volumes a_z. Let 0<sigma<=mu be a finite
submeasure, with fiber masses m_z and total m. Assume the centroid g_sigma
has integer base z_sigma. If a closed ambient cap H contains g_sigma, then

    vol_d(K_zsigma intersect H_zsigma)
        >=gamma_d [sum_z m_z^(1+1/d)/m]^d.               (1)

The selected centroid is an actual point of S by convexity. No mass from
outside the output fiber is counted on the left.

To prove this, first let the continuous part u of the cap normal be nonzero
and use the cap roots

    F(z,t)=vol_d{x in K_z:u.x+v.z>=t},       G=F^(1/d).

As proved in the preceding note, G is jointly concave on its positive
convex domain. The map x -> F(z,u.x+v.z) sends full uniform volume on K_z
to Lebesgue measure on [0,a_z]. Therefore its pushforward of sigma_z is
some measure eta_z dominated by Lebesgue measure on that interval, with
mass m_z. The elementary bathtub bound gives

    integral s^(1/d) d eta_z(s)
        >= integral_0^(m_z) s^(1/d)ds
        =[d/(d+1)]m_z^(1+1/d).                          (2)

Indeed write d eta_z=q(s)ds with 0<=q<=1. The product
(s^(1/d)-m_z^(1/d))(q(s)-1_[0,m_z](s)) is nonnegative everywhere;
its integral, using equality of the two masses, proves (2).

Apply Jensen to normalized sigma and then sum (2) over fibers. It yields

    G(z_sigma,u.x_sigma+v.z_sigma)
       >=[d/(d+1)] sum_z m_z^(1+1/d)/m.

The halfspace through this centroid and parallel to H is contained in H,
so raising to the dth power proves (1). The upper semicontinuity argument
in the preceding note handles all boundary mean points rigorously.

If u=0, Jensen for a(z)^(1/d) gives

    a_zsigma^(1/d)>=sum_z m_z a_z^(1/d)/m
                   >=sum_z m_z^(1+1/d)/m,

which is stronger than (1). Thus closed vertical caps carrying complete
fiber mass are also covered.

## 2. The exact maximum balanced mass inside one fiber

Let K be a positive d-dimensional convex body and let ell(x) be a
nonconstant affine functional. Define

    B(K,ell)=max{sigma(K): 0<=sigma<=1_K dx,
                              integral ell d sigma=0}. (3)

The maximum exists by weak compactness and continuity of ell. Suppose
first that integral_K ell<0. Let p=integral_{ell>0} ell dx. If p=0,
then B=0: the zero hyperplane has zero d-volume, and all remaining values
are negative. If p>0, then ell assumes both signs and the monotone
continuous function

    A(c)=integral_{K intersect {ell>=c}} ell dx,
              min_K ell<=c<=0,

is negative at the left endpoint and positive at 0. It is strictly
increasing while c lies in the interior negative projection range, since
removing a strip of strictly negative values strictly increases its
integral. Hence there is a unique c<0 with A(c)=0.

The maximizing submeasure in (3) is full uniform volume on

    D=K intersect {ell>=c}.                              (4)

To prove optimality, let sigma be any feasible submeasure and let tau be
uniform volume on D. On D, sigma-tau is nonpositive; outside D it is
nonnegative. Thus (ell-c)(sigma-tau) is a nonpositive signed integrand
in both regions. Integrating and using both zero moments gives

    -c [sigma(K)-tau(K)]<=0.

Because -c>0, sigma(K)<=tau(K). This proves (4), including attainment,
without a transport existence assumption. If integral_K ell>0, reverse
ell; the maximizing body is a lower cap. If the original mean is zero,
the entire fiber is maximizing.

In every positive-mass case the maximizing subbody is convex and its
ell-mean is zero. Ordinary Grunbaum or (1) therefore gives

    |K intersect {ell>=0}|>=gamma_d B(K,ell).            (5)

If any smaller mass s<=B is desired, scale the maximizing submeasure by
s/B; it remains dominated and balanced.

## 3. Exact three-fiber martingale peeling

Let the integer fibers at -1,0,1 be A,K,B with volumes a,b,a. Suppose the
actual mixed centroid is at base 0, and translate the tested cap functional
so that its mean over the whole mixed measure is zero and the cap is
{ell>=0}. The restriction ell_z to each fiber includes its integer-normal
coefficient. Put

    s_A=B(A,ell_-),         s_B=B(B,ell_+),
    s=min(s_A,s_B).

For every 0<=t<=s choose balanced endpoint submeasures of mass t using
Section 2. Remove them from the original measure. Their output centroids
have integer bases -1 and 1 and tested-functional mean zero. The residual
measure has total mass M-2t, fiber masses a-t,b,a-t, integer base mean 0,
and tested-functional mean zero. The equal peeling masses are exactly
what preserves its base mean.

Apply (1) separately to these three measures. Their output fibers are
distinct, so their cap lower bounds can be added without overlap. The
result is the rigorous tradeoff

    mu(H)>=gamma_d [2t+
        { [2(a-t)^(1+1/d)+b^(1+1/d)]/(M-2t) }^d],       (6)

for every such t, where M=2a+b. This is an attained, explicit optimization
of the displayed bound over the compact interval [0,s].

If both endpoint centroids lie strictly outside H, the middle centroid
lies inside H by the total centroid identity. Ordinary Grunbaum then
improves the middle term to the maximum of b and the braced quantity:

    mu(H)>=gamma_d [2t+max(b,
        { [2(a-t)^(1+1/d)+b^(1+1/d)]/(M-2t) }^d)].       (7)

Thus in the remaining nonheavy regime a<=b<2a, the concrete sufficient
condition

    min(B(A,ell_-),B(B,ell_+)) >=(2a-b)/4               (8)

proves the conditional OC cap bound gamma_d M/2, by choosing the right
side as t in (7). No assertion that (8) always holds is made.

Conversely, any decomposition using endpoint-output components with
integer output bases -1 and 1 must source those components solely from
the respective endpoint fibers, because those indices are extreme.
If a single residual component has base mean 0, the total masses assigned
to the two endpoints must agree. Their common mass is bounded by s through
(3). Hence [0,s] is the exact feasible interval for this particular
three-output balanced peeling scheme, not just a convenient sufficient
allocation interval.

These statements preserve every tested oblique halfspace through its
full affine functional ell. They do not impose a coordinate-only cap
restriction and do not assume that unrelated cap directions use the
same peeling decomposition.
